✓L∃∀N

The judgment \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma' states that the expression e, under the environment \rho and the store \sigma, has the result r and yields \sigma'. The result is \mathsf{lval}\,\ell for an lvalue, the location of the object it designates, and \mathsf{val}\,v for any other expression, Definition 2.1.7. The lvalues are a variable, an unqualified field of this, a dereferenced pointer, a field of an object, a field through a pointer, a call of a member that returns a reference, an element of a vector, and a conditional whose chosen branch is one. The store enters expressions because a call or a new inside an expression may change it.

One judgment serves both the value and the location of an expression, as in the L‑values and R‑values of Strachey (1967, reprinted in Higher‑Order and Symbolic Computation 13, 2000). The context decides, by the conversion rd of Definition 2.1.7.

The judgment \rho, \sigma \vdash c \Rightarrow r, \rho', \sigma' states that the command c yields the control r, the environment \rho' and the store \sigma'. The output environment exists so that a declaration extends \rho for the following commands, and the block discards the extension and frees its owned locations when it ends.

```
────────────────────────── (Seq-Empty)
```

```
ρ, σ ⊢ c ⇒ normal, ρ₁, σ₁    ρ₁, σ₁ ⊢ cs ⇒ r, ρ₂, σ₂

ρ, σ ⊢ c cs ⇒ r, ρ₂, σ₂
```

The evaluator runs in the monad M, which carries the trace of the derivation. When tracing is on, each rule application records the instance of the rule it concludes, or the error, at its depth in the tree, with the antecedent and the consequent in parts. The trace records a premise of the library under the rule of its module, such as V-New, the creation of a vector in Definition 8.2.1, or F-New, the creation of a function object in Definition 8.2.2. The state survives the error, so the trace keeps the rule applications up to the failing rule. The log holds the instances in post order, each premise before its conclusion.

The function renderTrace rebuilds the tree from the log. It lays the tree out as a derivation on the board, the premises over a line of inference, the conclusion under it and the rule name at the right.

A legend names the environments \rho_i, the stores \sigma_j and the subjects longer than 40 characters, so every judgment fits one line. The function writes a subtree wider than 100 columns apart, under a name \mathcal{D}_k.

Let n \le m. A result of a function of the evaluator with fuel n that is not the error outOfFuel is its result with fuel m, from the same arguments and the same state of the monad M. The value or the error, the trace and the state after the run coincide. In particular run p n \neq outOfFuel implies run p m = run p n.

Proof for Theorem 2.4.4
uses 0

The proof is by induction on n, for all the functions of the evaluator at once, in CoreCpp/Semantics/FuelMono.lean. The relation LeP compares two runs, and its congruence lemmas cover sequencing, the caught errors, traced, tracedLib, tracedCases, the conditional and the loops of for. With fuel 0 every function gives outOfFuel, and the statement holds vacuously. With fuel n + 1 and m + 1 the two bodies coincide except for the fuel of the recursive calls, where the induction hypothesis applies. A run that does not end in outOfFuel has no recursive call that ends in it, because every error that a body catches, in traced and in the cases of tracedCases, the body throws again. The theorem of Radix, Stmt.interp_fuel_mono, covers the successful results only. This one covers the errors too, which the search for the least fuel of Theorem 2.4.8 needs.

A value of a function of the evaluator has a derivation in the relation of its judgement, for every fuel and every state of the monad M. A value (r, \sigma') of expr on \rho, \sigma and e gives a derivation of \rho, \sigma \vdash e \Rightarrow r, \sigma'. The same holds for cmd, cmds and the auxiliary functions. In particular runMain p n = ok v implies p \Rightarrow v. The statement holds for every program, well typed or not. Radix states it for its commands as Stmt.interp_sound.

Proof for Theorem 2.4.5
uses 0

The proof is by induction on n, for all the functions of the evaluator at once, in CoreCpp/Semantics/InterpSound.lean. The predicate Ok c P states that every value of the computation c satisfies P. Its lemmas cover sequencing, the caught errors, traced, tracedLib, tracedCases and the loops of for. Each case of a function builds the rule its comment names from the induction hypothesis on the premises. The loops of Call and Member build Bind from the last parameter back, and the loops of applyVals give the allocations of Apply. A function of CoreCpp.Std gives a derivation in the relation of its module. The evaluator collects the owned locations in reverse order, and \sigma \setminus L depends only on the elements of L.

The proof exposed one divergence of the evaluator from CallLib. The rule requires (f, k) in libDecls for a call with k arguments, and the evaluator checked the name alone. A header that declared assert with two parameters thus let assert(true) give a value with no derivation. The evaluator now checks the arity and gives the guard arity otherwise.

Proof for Theorem 2.4.6
uses 0

The proof is one mutual structural recursion on the derivation, in CoreCpp/Semantics/InterpComplete.lean. The predicate Done c a states that the computation c gives a from every state. A rule whose premises the functions reach with fuels n_i is reached with fuel 1 + \sum n_i, or 2 + \sum n_i where a premise is the method lookup or the field lookup, and with any larger fuel. The loops of Call, Member, New and Delete follow the derivations of Bind, Ctors and Dtors one element at a time. The relations of the library give a value of the function of their module.

The proof exposed one divergence of the relation from CallLib. The rule requires that f is no function of the program, and the relation required only that no function named f has the chosen signature. A program with a function and a header declaration of one name thus had a derivation that the evaluator did not reach. The relation now requires p.funsNamed f = [], as T-CallLib does.

Let p pass prepare and run p b \neq outOfFuel. The search leastFuel p b gives the least fuel d with run p d \neq outOfFuel. So d \le b, run p d \neq outOfFuel, and run p j = outOfFuel for every j < d.

Proof for Theorem 2.4.8
uses 0

The search doubles an upper bound from 1 until the program does not exhaust it, capped at b, and then halves the interval between the last exhausted fuel and that bound. Both phases keep two invariants. The lower end exhausts the fuel and the upper end does not. Fuel 0 exhausts it, since every function of the evaluator gives outOfFuel with fuel 0. The binary search stops at an interval (d - 1, d]. By Theorem 2.4.4, a fuel that exhausts the evaluator makes every smaller fuel exhaust it too, so every j \le d - 1 exhausts it.
